class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>It’s difficult to summarize Williams’ role in the creation of “To Leave You” and its kin with a one-word job title such as “choreographer. In assembling artists of several stripes and guiding their creativity with her prompts, she could be called a director, engineer or even a conductor.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Barry Brecheisen/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Williams often finds nontraditional dance venues, entertaining even a Chinese restaurant for “To Leave You.” She landed on Three Top Lounge at the Salt Shed, responding to some alchemy of the decor, the views and the openness. "There was just something that I was like, 'Oh, this is the place,'" she said.</p><p>In developing “To Leave You,” Williams and the other artists followed paths that presented themselves to them. Similarly, “To Leave You” itself was a path that appeared after Williams’ two most recent pieces. “Echo Mine” was inspired by the dancer Claire Bataille, who became ill and passed away before the piece premiered. Then “Hisako’s House” explored the legacy Williams’ grandmother left her, and was performed on-site in her grandmother’s house in Lombard. Hisako, too, died before the premiere. The meditations on mortality that arose from those two artistically entwined deaths sparked “To Leave You.”</p><p>At the lounge inside the Salt Shed, the audience will move around as the performance unfolds, promenade-style. “Like stepping into the world from the get-go, with us,” Williams said. Another boundary made permeable. Who knows what future works will emerge from the embers of this one?</p>

entries.title: "Once Upon a Time in Harlem" documentary introduces audiences to Chicago journalist Gerri Major
entries.summary: <p>At the height of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s, the city bustled with activity.</p><p>People recited Langston Hughes’ “Weary Blues” poem on street corners. Duke Ellington delivered electrifying performances at the Cotton Club. A'Lelia Walker, daughter of millionaire Madam C. J. Walker, drew an enviable guest list to salons at her townhouse.</p><p>There to capture it all was Gerri Major, a glamorous journalist and Chicago native whose columns covered the Black upper class until her death at 90 years old in 1984. Nicknamed the “Harlem hostess,” she wrote for several newspapers before becoming a senior editor at Ebony and the society editor at Jet magazine.</p><p>Major is a central figure in “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” William and David Greaves’ critically acclaimed documentary playing in select Chicago theaters in November. The film, featured in the <a class="Link" href="https://web.saic.edu/blackharvestfest/" target="_blank" ><u>Black Harvest Film Festival</u></a> running Nov. 6-15 at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago’s Gene Siskel Film Center, captures a party attended by Major, composer Eubie Blake, painter Aaron Douglas and more than 20 other Harlem Renaissance luminaries at Duke Ellington’s home in 1972.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-050000" name="image-050000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” Gerri Major describes herself as a “helpful” journalist to the Black community. “If I had a choice of saying something that would hurt our people or keeping quiet, I would keep quiet.” </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Carl Van Vechten Papers/Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Major’s body of work is a detailed chronicle of Black life, history and genealogy, but she has remained an obscure figure — until now.</p><p>“She was an important journalist in terms of just raising the profile of what was happening with the people during that time,” said Liani Greaves, who is David’s daughter and one of the documentary’s producers. “The purpose of our film is to tell those stories to insert the renaissance into the cultural memory of the nation.”</p><p>Also a fashion icon, Major has <a class="Link" href="https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/collection/search?edan_q=%2A%3A%2A&edan_fq%5B%5D=name%3A%22Major%2C%2BGerri%22&op=Search" target="_blank" ><u>a dress</u></a> featured in the National Museum of African American History and Culture’s collection. She is a regal presence in “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” adorned in gold necklaces and bracelets and green rings that match her flower-patterned dress. In the documentary, she converses warmly with the other guests, including other Chicago natives: librarian Regina Andrews, historian Nathan Huggins and activist Louise Patterson.</p><p>Major also reminisces about throwing her own lavish parties at her home on West 139th Street, the cultural mecca known as “Strivers’ Row,” as well as her career.</p><p>She describes herself as a “helpful journalist” rather than a “great journalist.”</p><p>“If I had a choice of saying something that would hurt our people or keeping quiet, I would keep quiet,” she says in the film. “If I couldn’t do something that was going to give us a boost up, I was never going to give us a boost down.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In 1953, Gerri Major joined the staff of magazines Ebony and Jet, covering major events such as the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in England. She is pictured here in 1972 in a still from “Once Upon a Time in Harlem.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Neon</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Born Geraldyn Hodges in 1894, her exposure to Black socialites began in her childhood in the Douglas community area. She was given a debutante ball at 18 and earned a bachelor’s degree in philosophy at the University of Chicago. But her early life wasn’t without struggle, especially as one of few Black women at the college.</p><p>“We were humiliated and put down and crucified, but we stuck it out,” she says in the film.</p><p>Before moving to Harlem, she married Dr. Henry Binga Dismond, the first of her three husbands, and taught at Stephen A. Douglas Elementary School. She also participated on a commission to investigate the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-history/2025/11/08/chicago-race-riot-1919-memorial-loop" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Race Riot of 1919</u></a>.</p><p>Besides reporting for the New York Amsterdam News, Pittsburgh Courier and other outlets, she worked as a publicist, radio announcer and writer with New York’s public health department.</p><p>In 1953, she joined the staff of magazines Ebony and Jet, owned by the Chicago-based Johnson Publishing Company. She traveled frequently, covering the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in England, writing about a dictator in the Dominican Republic and overseeing the company’s Paris bureau. Her column for Jet, “Gerri Major’s Society World,” ran until her death.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a the 1976 book, “Black Society,” tracing the evolution of the Black upper class from the 1700s to contemporary times.</p><p>William Greaves initially sat on the “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” footage while continuing to shoot more content about the renaissance. After he died in 2014, his family worked to restore and release the film.</p><p>David Greaves, William's son, said it was important to share the stories of Major and others in the documentary at a time when Black history is being removed from schools and other institutions.</p><p>Seeing the film is “an act of resistance,” he added.</p><p>Major also felt her life was a lesson for younger generations.</p><p>“They have to remember that there are those of us who are now old, who have struggled, and worked hard, and had little to work with, had little sympathy, had no civil rights, had nothing, and we struggled and went ahead and worked and some of us died doing it,” she says in the film.</p><p>“And if they cross us all off, they’ve lost a great thing.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Justine Tobiasz</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e20000" name="module-e20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Where Chicago audiences can see “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” </b><br><br><b>Music Box Theatre </b><br>Beginning Nov. 9<br>3733 N. entries.title: Flock, maker of controversial license plate readers, starts to give campaign cash to local politicians
entries.summary: <p>Flock Safety license plate reading cameras have spread throughout the Chicago area, stirring controversy about surveillance and civil liberties while helping snare crooks.</p><p>The company’s money has also begun to spread to local politics, according to election records.</p><p>In Cicero, where Flock has a number of cameras monitoring traffic, the Atlanta company has given several campaign contributions to Town President Larry Dominick, who oversees public safety in the near west suburb.</p><p>The first contribution to the Cicero Voters Alliance (The Larry Dominick Team) was for $1,000, made in 2021, according to Illinois State Board of Elections records.</p><p>In 2022 another $1,000 arrived from Flock, while in 2024 the company gave $2,000.</p><p>In 2025, the year Dominick successfully ran for reelection, Flock gave him another $2,000.</p><p>The community now has 31 Flock cameras, and first engaged the company in or about 2020, a town spokesman said.</p><p>“The Town of Cicero is proud of the hundreds of crimes solved with the help of Flock cameras and our officers would be utilizing them to help keep the community safe with or without the $6,000 they’ve contributed to President Dominick over the last six years,” the spokesman said.</p><p>Dominick appears to be the only local municipal leader to have received Flock campaign cash so far. But the company did donate to two candidates for sheriff in the collar counties.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a technology.</p><p>Idleburg handily won reelection on Tuesday against Buchberger.</p><p>Flock officials didn’t respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Records show Flock employs two firms to lobby on its behalf in Illinois, including Cozen O’Connor Public Strategies, which is affiliated with a Philadelphia law firm and appears to have been hired by Flock in early 2024.</p><p>Since then, the company has given around $485,000 in campaign money to state and local candidates and political causes, according to elections board records that show employees or consultants of Cozen O’Connor gave an additional $14,000 during the same time frame.</p><p>Cozen O’Connor also represents several dozen other clients in Illinois, from the rideshare company Lyft to Planned Parenthood of Illinois and <a >Catholic Charities</a>, Starbucks and the YMCA of Metropolitan Chicago, state records show.</p><p>National Strategies LLC, which is based in Washington, D.C., and serves as another Flock lobbying firm in Illinois, didn’t report any donations to state or local campaign accounts, though members of the business have donated to numerous federal campaigns.</p><p>As <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/15/lobbyists-campaign-contributions-juliana-stratton-us-senate-general-election" target="_blank" >the Chicago Sun-Times has reported</a>, Flock has used the bipartisan firm Mercury Public Affairs for federal lobbying, and members of the firm have given campaign money to — and participated in a campaign fundraiser for — Juliana Stratton in her run for U.S. Senate.</p><p>Flock CEO Garrett Langley gave a $1,000 contribution in 2024 to a campaign fund benefiting U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) target="_blank" >Fran Spielman</a></h5><p><b>North Side tragedy</b>: A fire tore through a Rogers Park townhome early Thursday, killing a family of four, including a 13-year-old, and their dog, officials said.</p><p><b>The victims</b>: The boy was identified as 8th-grader Valentino Vallejo in an email to families from his school. pandemic, the Jan. 6, 2021 insurrection, the Supreme Court's decision to strike down Roe v. Wade, the 2023 mayoral election, the 2024 Democratic National Convention, Operation Midway Blitz and much more.</p><p>Simons became the host of WBEZ's morning news and talk show "In the Loop" in September 2025 and is the only Chicago journalist with a regular sit-down with Mayor Brandon Johnson, the monthly series "Ask The Mayor."</p><p>"Leading 'Reset' and now 'In the Loop' has been one of the great privileges of my career," Simons said. "I am truly thankful for the Chicagoans who welcomed me into their lives and trusted me with their stories, questions and hopes for this city. obscurity in acclaimed documentary</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddukykt-l-th/" target="_blank" >Erica Thompson</a></h5><p>At the height of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s, the city bustled with activity.</p><p>There to capture it all was Gerri Major, a glamorous journalist and Chicago native whose columns covered the Black upper class until her death at 90 years old in 1984. Nicknamed the "Harlem hostess," she wrote for several newspapers before becoming a senior editor at Ebony and the society editor at Jet magazine.</p><p>Major is a central figure in "Once Upon a Time in Harlem," William and David Greaves’ critically acclaimed documentary playing in select Chicago theaters in November.</p><p>The film, featured in the <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddukykt-l-tk/" target="_blank" >Black Harvest Film Festival</a> that's running Friday through Nov. 15 at the School of the Gene Siskel Film Center, captures a party attended by Major, composer Eubie Blake, painter Aaron Douglas and more than 20 other Harlem Renaissance luminaries at Duke Ellington's home in 1972.</p><p>Born Geraldyn Hodges in 1894, her exposure to Black socialites began in her childhood in the Douglas community area. She was given a debutante ball at 18 and earned a bachelor's degree in philosophy at the University of Chicago.</p><p>Major's body of work is a detailed chronicle of Black life, history and genealogy, but she has remained an obscure figure — until now.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddukykt-l-tu/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>Yesterday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddukykt-l-ir/" target="_blank" >After Tuesday’s nationwide wins, what is your message to Democrats as they prepare to take control of the House and Senate?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said, edited for length and clarity:</p><p>"Don't f--- it up. Take care of your constituents, work with your colleagues in Congress, be decent. The best reelection campaign is a good record." — <i>Phoebe M.</i></p><p>"Affordability and accountability. You don’t have to choose one over the other. Do both." — <i>Thomas Rodriguez</i></p><p>"Small standalone bills that 70% of the country wants. Oversight, keep the borders tight but get rid of ICE inside our country, stop the war, forget impeachment you don't have the votes, [lower] drug prices and fix the insurance nightmare." — <i>Caryn Seidman</i></p><p>"Focus on governing. Put investigations on the back burner. Forget about impeachments. Pass dozens of single-topic clean bills that force Republicans to vote on each issue and then, if passed, force Trump to sign or veto. Implement the things that are needed to make the lives of ordinary Americans better. Deliver actual results." — <i>Usha Gupta</i></p><p>"People want results. Don’t think that Texas and Kansas suddenly became California. People didn’t become MAGA two years ago, and they’re not DSA now. The pendulum will keep swinging until someone gets it right." — <i>John Paul</i></p><hr><p></p><h4>PICTURE CHICAGO 📸</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Electric scooter driver, 67, killed in collision with speeding SUV in North Park
entries.summary: <p>In the second fatal electric scooter crash in as many days, a 67-year-old man scooter driver has died after a collision with a speeding SUV early Friday in the North Park neighborhood on the Northwest Side. </p><p>The stand-up scooter driver, an unidentified 67-year-old man, was in the intersection of the 3300 block of West Peterson Avenue around 4:35 a.m. when a Dodge SUV "made contact" with him, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Saint Francis Hospital in Evanston where he was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>The Dodge driver was cited for speeding.</p><p>Another electric scooter driver was<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/05/electric-scooter-driver-dead-after-collision-with-cpd-vehicle-in-bridgeport" target="_blank" > killed in a crash</a> early Thursday after a collision with a Chicago police vehicle in Bridgeport. </p><p>In that accident, officers were on patrol in a marked police vehicle, traveling north on Princeton Avenue where they “came into contact” with a stand-up electric scooter operated by a 39-year-old male at 32nd Street, police said in a statement.</p><p>The still-unidentified scooter operator suffered injuries to his body and was taken to Stroger Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said.</p>

entries.title: Man facing attempted murder charges after shooting boy, 17, in Gresham police say
entries.summary: <p>A man is due in court Friday accused of shooting a 17-year-old boy in Gresham earlier this week. </p><p>Dennis Cain, 32, was arrested several hours after the Tuesday shooting and charged with attempted murder, aggravated battery, aggravated assault and possessing a weapon as a felon, Chicago police said. </p><p>Cain, of the 8600 block of South Muskegon Avenue, allegedly unlawfully entered a home around 12:50 a.m. Tuesday in the 7700 block of South Lowe Avenue and shot the teen in the back, police said. </p><p>A 12-year-old was also in the home at the home but wasn't hurt. </p><p>Cain was expected to appear in court Friday. </p>

entries.title: 3 shot when bullets smash through window of Englewood apartment
entries.summary: <p>Gunfire ripped through an apartment window and hit three people inside the Englewood apartment early Friday on the South Side,</p><p>Two women, 21 and 23, were inside an apartment when the shooting happened around 1:10 a.m. in the 400 block of West Marquette Road, Chicago police said. </p><p>They were both shot in the legs and were taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where they were in fair condition, police said. </p><p>A 21-year-old man was shot in the chest and took himself to the Little Company of Mary Hospital where he was in good condition, officials said. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Why Tyler Bertuzzi's goal-scoring has disappeared for Blackhawks this season
entries.summary: <p>TAMPA, Fla. — When the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> set higher expectations for the 2026-27 season, they were counting on most of their established players repeating their 2025-26 performances and some up-and-coming players taking big steps forward.</p><p>The latter has happened. Touted rookie forwards Roman Kantserov and Anton Frondell and enigmatic second-year defenseman Artyom Levshunov have been three bright spots.</p><p>The former, however, has not happened across the board. Spencer Knight's save percentage has dropped from .902 to .892, and his analytics depict an exactly league-average goalie so far. Patrick Kane hasn't scored since the season opener — but had taken seven minor penalties between then and getting injured Monday.</p><p>And Tyler Bertuzzi, who led the Hawks with 32 goals last season, is stuck on just two goals this season — one of which was an empty-netter.</p><p>"Sometimes they go in, sometimes they don't," Bertuzzi said recently. "I feel like I haven't been able to get as many grade-A chances, and then some games I'm getting a lot of chances. If you're getting chances, that's a good thing. Eventually they'll go in. [You] just have to keep creating chances. I'm looking for those spots to get open."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Tyler Bertuzzi has uncharacteristically missed some tap-ins this season, like this one against the Kings: <a href="https://t.co/JvvXDHuaHP">pic.twitter.com/JvvXDHuaHP</a></p>— Ben Pope’s Video Clips (@BenPopeCSTclips) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCSTclips/status/2118585502609691056?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 6, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The 31-year-old winger seems like a particularly poor fit in coach Jeff Blashill's high-pressure system, which is designed to take advantage of the Hawks' team speed.</p><p>That speed is prevalent in most of their young forwards (and on-the-way prospects). But Bertuzzi, on the other hand, is one of the NHL's slowest skaters.</p><p>In the Hawks' aggressive 2-1-2 forecheck, the puck is often gone before he gets low enough to pressure opposing defensemen, and then he's caught chasing the play back up the ice.</p><p>TNT panelist Paul Bissonnette <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/04/blackhawks-panthers-tnt-paul-bissonnette-connor-bedard" >ripped</a> Bertuzzi for a poor forecheck during the first period Wednesday against the Panthers, but a more effective Bertuzzi forecheck did help create Roman Kantserov's second-period goal. Bertuzzi later said he thinks the Hawks' forecheck has improved recently.</p><p>"Our [defensemen] are down the walls a lot more, and we're keeping pucks alive," Bertuzzi added. "Sometimes we can get a little bit in-between. We've got to be fast-paced, just on top of everyone."</p><p>The fact most of the Hawks' scarce offense comes off the rush rather than from offensive-zone cycles — plus that most of their cycle chances are one-and-done because they struggle to retrieve loose pucks — particularly hurts Bertuzzi, too.</p><p>He's one of the league's most efficient finishers around the net, but that relies on teammates getting the puck to the net. If they don't, the so-called "human backboard" isn't as useful.</p><p>During five-on-five play, Bertuzzi is averaging just 6.5 shot attempts per 60 minutes, down from 10.7 last season. And on the power play, he's averaging 10.8 attempts per 60, down from 18.6. He was taken off the top power-play unit this week for the first time all season.</p><p>"We've got to do a better job of getting more pucks...for him to get opportunities for rebound looks, tip looks, things like that," Blashill said recently. "That's not on him; that's on our team. Right now, we're just not generating enough across the board."</p><p>Even when the Hawks do generate close-in chances for Bertuzzi, he isn't finishing them at his usual rate. Only 47.2% of his attempts have made it successfully on-goal (down from 55.4% last season) and only 5.5% have gone in (down from 10.8%).</p><p>Bad luck is a contributing factor, and that should balance out over time, even if the systemic issues will take more effort to resolve. He has had several should-have-been tap-ins shockingly skitter wide in recent games.</p><p>"It just needs to cross the red line," he said. "I'll keep going to the net. I'm not too worried about it."</p>

entries.title: City decision to reject General Iron permit upheld by appellate court
entries.summary: <p>The city’s decision to deny a Southeast Side metal-shredding business an operating permit because of concerns over air pollution and public health was upheld by a state appellate court Friday.</p><p>The relocated and rebranded General Iron scrap metal operation was built and ready to open at East 116th Street along the Calumet River when then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot’s administration <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/2/18/22940770/southeast-side-metal-shredder-chicago-rejects-plan-open-general-iron-relocation" >rejected the permit</a>, citing the potential public health impact from air pollution.</p><p>The owner of the business argued that the city didn’t follow its own rules when it made the decision to reject the business permit. The owner, known as General III, was allowed to build its facility because it received a construction permit from the state.</p><p>General Iron operated in Lincoln Park for decades even as the neighborhood around it gentrified. Developers, city officials and neighbors who viewed the business as a nuisance pushed for the business to move.</p><p>When it was announced that the business would move to Latino-majority East Side, there was an uproar across the Southeast Side. Community, health and environmental advocates mobilized and pressured Lightfoot to deny the permit.</p><p>A federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/5/12/23720343/hud-environmental-racism-lightfoot-general-iron-environmental-justice-housing-urban-development" >civil rights investigation</a> found that moving the business from a white community and into a Latino neighborhood surrounded by predominantly Black communities was discriminatory.</p><p>Reserve Management Group, the majority owner of General III, has argued that the city added a health impact assessment late in the permit-decision process and it was beyond the scope of the application review. It then asked a city administrative law judge to consider whether the business had met its requirements for the permit.</p><p>That city judge sided with General III, which prompted Mayor Brandon Johnson’s administration to challenge that decision in circuit court.</p><p>In August 2024, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2024/08/16/general-iron-brandon-johnson-judge-rules-permit-air-pollution" >the circuit court ruled</a> the city acted within its right to deny the permit. The business then appealed that decision to the three-judge First District Illinois Appellate Court, which has now upheld the permit denial again.</p><p>The business takes junked cars, large appliances and other sources to salvage metal and resell it.</p><p>In a statement, the business, which was to be rebranded Southside Recycling, said it will take its case to the Illinois Supreme Court.</p><p>“Our environmentally friendly state-of-the-art facility meets all applicable city, state and federal environmental and public health standards,” the statement said. “We remain fully committed to obtaining the operating permit.”</p><p>A city law department spokeswoman didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.<br></p>

entries.title: Will the Illinois House elect its first woman speaker? Dems float potential contenders to replace Welch
entries.summary: <p>After this week’s bombshell announcement that Illinois’ first Black House speaker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/05/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-mutiny-26-democrats-call-for-new-leader-harry-benton-scandal" target="_blank" ><u>wouldn’t seek a fourth term</u></a>, Democratic state legislators could blaze another new trail with their selection for the next leader of their chamber.</p><p>Five women lawmakers were among the names floated most frequently as the Sun-Times spoke on background with more than a dozen lawmakers, lobbyists and other insiders sizing up potential candidates to replace outgoing House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, D-Hillside.</p><p>Many said it was time for Illinois to see its first woman speaker to help uproot an entrenched culture of sexual harassment following the Capitol’s latest scandal.</p><p>Welch lost the support of most of his caucus in the wake of his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" target="_blank" ><u>delayed response</u></a> to misconduct allegations against disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield — just like Welch’s longtime predecessor, imprisoned ex-Speaker Michael Madigan, was felled amid criticism of his inaction on complaints within his political organization.</p><p>There has scarcely been a question about the occupancy of the speaker’s office since Madigan first tightened his iron grip on the gavel in 1983. And even for a brief interlude of Republican House control in 1995-96, Lee Daniels was a clear pick to shift from GOP minority leader.</p><p>Now, for the first time in four decades, legislators have adequate time to seriously consider a field of representatives to step up in their chamber, without an incumbent or another obvious power player towering over the election for speaker.</p><p>Welch was a late entry in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/13/22228758/emanuel-chris-welch-illinois-house-speaker-vote-mike-madigan" target="_blank" ><u>the 2021 intra-party race</u></a> after Madigan’s stunning announcement he was stepping down, prompting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/12/22227890/sources-latinx-caucus-latino-welch-hispanic-house-speaker-black-madigan-hernandez-williams-kifowit" target="_blank" ><u>a chaotic scramble for votes</u></a> over the final day of a lame-duck legislative session — a power grab that didn’t even play out in the Capitol itself. Lawmakers were masked and socially distanced in a Springfield convention center in the depths of the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>“By the time [Madigan] suspended his campaign, there were 24 hours for us to make a decision,” said North Side state Rep. Kelly Cassidy, one of the legislators who led the movement for new leadership. “That’s not a healthy way for us to do this.</p><p>“We have an actual chance to put thought into this that we didn’t get to before, and to hear from our colleagues about their visions. We have such an array of experience and talent throughout every corner of our caucus,” Cassidy said — noting she’s “not even remotely” interested in the post herself.</p><p>Asked if it’s time for a female speaker, Gov. JB Pritzker said “that's going to be up to the members.”</p><p>“What I know is that anybody who has been sexually harassed or had anything like that happen to them should know what the process is for reporting that,” Pritzker said at an unrelated news conference Friday. “The House is really responsible for getting their house in order… Every company, every nonprofit, virtually everybody I know, has developed a process for their institutions to deal with these things.  It should be no different for the House Representatives.”</p><p>Maneuvering behind closed doors will accelerate during the fall veto session that starts Nov. 17, reaching a political crescendo with the speaker's election in January immediately after the 105th General Assembly is sworn in.</p><p>The Sun-Times identified just one hat officially thrown into the ring by Friday morning, but plenty more will be in the weeks ahead. entries.title: Roman Kantserov not letting Blackhawks' losing ways weigh him down
entries.summary: <p>RALEIGH, N.C. — Roman Kantserov's last-minute goal Thursday was meaningless for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> but significant for him.</p><p>It extended his point streak to seven consecutive games — the longest by a Hawks rookie since Jonathan Toews in 2007 — and kept him atop the NHL rookie goal-scoring leaderboard. He's now at eight goals, just ahead of three high-profile first-round picks: Trevor Connelly, James Hagens and Gavin McKenna.</p><p>Amazingly, though, the Hawks have only won one of those seven games. Kantserov has factored in nearly half — seven of 15 — of their total goals during the stretch. His teammates are barely producing anything at all.</p><p>"Regardless of how it’s going for everybody else, it seems to be working for him right now," Ryan Donato said Thursday. "I hope that we can help him out and...he can continue to stay hot, and then we can have another couple guys get hot, as well."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">GOAL: Roman Kantserov chips in a loose puck to get the Blackhawks on the board. <a href="https://t.co/FkFJatLzGI">pic.twitter.com/FkFJatLzGI</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2118164842972401764?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>These team struggles represent one of many American culture shocks for the 22-year-old Russian forward, who isn't accustomed to losing.</p><p>Magnitogorsk Metallurg, his hometown KHL team that he played for before making the NHL jump this summer, is a perennial power.</p><p>They posted records of 44-24, 43-25 and 44-24 in each of Kantserov's three seasons, obviously making the playoffs every year and winning the KHL championship his first year. That's not out of the ordinary, considering they've posted only losing season since at least 1997 (and likely longer).</p><p>The Hawks, on the other hand, have dwelled in the NHL basement throughout that time.</p><p>"It's a little bit different because, before NHL, I played always on contending teams [that were] going to make the playoffs," Kantserov said this week, adding he has "the mentality of a winning guy."</p><p>"Now I have same mentality, but we just need to stay focused. We have the time. We need just to give up our stupid mistakes and focus on our game. Because the team is young but everybody is skilled. I hope, in a couple weeks, we stay [getting] better. It should be fine."</p><p>He believes he's doing a good job not letting the losses weigh too heavily on his mind. </p><p>"For sure it's sad when you lose, but you just focus on your health, analyze your game, watch a couple shifts, [see how] you can play better and forget about the last game and be ready for the next one," he said.</p><p>"Because there's so many games here. It will not be [smart] to think about, 'Oh my God, I can play better. I can't score here.' You have a new game, new chances."</p><p>He has scored on one of out every seven shot attempts so far, and his shooting percentage is an otherworldly 27.6%, which is unsustainable and will inevitably decline. </p><p>But there's reason to believe it should remain well above the league average of 11%. He finished with a 20.8% shooting percentage in the KHL last season, for what that's worth.</p><p>Kantserov isn't solely a net-mouth fiend like Tyler Bertuzzi, but he does understand the importance of stopping in the dangerous areas and looking around. That's how he scored Wednesday against the Panthers: he was simply there when the puck ended up there.</p><p>"If you look at a lot of his goals, they are around the net," coach Jeff Blashill said. "He's not going to score from far out, but he's a smart player. He's good around the net. He's got good eye-hand coordination so he can tip pucks. He's a good shooter."</p><p>Blashill added he didn't think Kantserov's line with Bertuzzi and Connor Bedard had as much "jump" Thursday as they did Wednesday. But it's a testament to Blashill's faith that Kantserov has been Bedard's most common linemate by far this season.</p><p>Kantserov has also shown flashes of ability to play a physical brand of hockey — a mentality the Hawks want to embrace more team-wide moving forward.</p>

entries.title: Bears report: RB Kyle Monangai practices for first time in more than a month
entries.summary: <p>What happened Friday at Halas Hall:</p><p><b>Monangai returns to practice</b><br><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> No. 2 running back Kyle Monangai practiced Friday for the first time in more than a month after hurting his toe in the Week 4 win over the Jets, when he rushed a career-high 30 times and finished with 146 yards and two touchdowns.</p><p>He was limited in practice and it seems unlikely that he’ll play Sunday against the Buccaneers, but the Bears listed him as questionable. With the bye week coming up, Monangai would get two more weeks to recover before facing the Saints on Nov. 22 by sitting out Sunday.</p><p><b>Jarrett likely to play</b><br>The Bears’ injuries have been a little tougher to gauge this week, coach Ben Johnson said, because of the quick turnaround <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/02/bears-big-plan-coming-together-beautifully-as-34-17-win-over-seahawks-pushes-them-to-best-start-since-2012" >returning from Seattle</a> on Tuesday and not holding a normal practice until Thursday.</p><p>He mentioned that specifically when asked about defensive tackle Grady Jarrett, who has missed time with a groin injury, but expected him to play against the Buccaneers.</p><p><b>Cornerback concerns</b><br>Bears cornerbacks Tyrique Stevenson (thumb) and Malik Muhammad (toe) have been pressing through injuries, but both were limited in practice Friday and listed as questionable for the game.</p><p><b>Benedet to play</b><br>Bears left tackle Theo Benedet injured his shoulder in the win over the Seahawks on Monday, but practiced in full Friday and was cleared to play.</p><p><b>Bucs’ updates</b><br>The Bucs ruled out starting outside linebacker Yaya Diaby and listed wide receiver Emeka Egbuka (foot) as questionable, though Egbuka practiced in full Thursday and Friday.</p><p>Left tackle Tristan Wirfs (toe) and safety Tykee Smith (ankle) will play.</p><p><b>Vacation plans?</b><br>When asked how many days, if any, he will take off during the bye week, Johnson said, “As much as my wife wants me to... I'll find out after the game what she wants to do, but if we're in town, it's going to be hard not to come [to Halas Hall] for at least a little bit.”</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: From Kenwood to Washington, an inside look at Illinois’ newest senator, Juliana Stratton
entries.summary: <p>Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton is best known for her work as lieutenant governor, her “F- - - - Trump” campaign slogan and for being a proud South Sider.</p><p>But she’s also a Beyoncé fan and a self-proclaimed “house head,” which was on full display election night as Stratton <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfTn4anOV1Z/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&psln=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==&srtk=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==" target="_blank" >showed off her dance moves</a> to Cajmere’s 1992 Chicago house classic, "Percolator."</p><p>Here are some things you may not know about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-senate-illinois-midterm-results" target="_blank" >Illinois’ newest senator</a>, who alongside Sen. Tammy Duckworth will make Illinois the first state in U.S. history to have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/juliana-strattons-win-marks-historic-first-for-women-of-color-in-national-politics" >two women of color</a> serving simultaneously in the U.S. Senate.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1a0000" name="image-1a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/934875e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7016x3938+0+371/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3b%2F89%2F25f6623c4ca1b0b415fa5516d19c%2Fday2pritzker-261105-25.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/54340e6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7016x3938+0+371/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3b%2F89%2F25f6623c4ca1b0b415fa5516d19c%2Fday2pritzker-261105-25.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/84f5e41/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7016x3938+0+371/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3b%2F89%2F25f6623c4ca1b0b415fa5516d19c%2Fday2pritzker-261105-25.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton hugs U.S. Sen. She now runs along the Lakefront Trail, bikes to yoga at Millennium Park and goes to Studio Yogi in the South Shore neighborhood. She's also a meditation fan. </p><h3><b>‘House head’</b></h3><p>She is a “house head” and left a campaign event in late October to head to a house dance party. Stratton said she wants to host a house dance party in Washington for other “house head” colleagues in Congress. Stratton goes to house music parties at Visions Odeum and Events in West Pullman.</p><h3><b>Queen Bey</b></h3><p>Stratton is a “major” Beyoncé fan and has a placard on her desk that reads “What would Beyoncé do?” She was also in the audience for an Oprah Winfrey show that featured Beyoncé and was so lively that the show’s producers asked her to come back to be part of the audience.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ea0000" name="image-ea0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/458c24c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3289x1846+0+240/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2Fd4%2F5617f7474faf8c845ed0ac46a30d%2F2181093703.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0dccf22/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3289x1846+0+240/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2Fd4%2F5617f7474faf8c845ed0ac46a30d%2F2181093703.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ab3e485/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3289x1846+0+240/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2Fd4%2F5617f7474faf8c845ed0ac46a30d%2F2181093703.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="HOUSTON, TEXAS - One of her cases was between a teenager who vandalized a store and the store owner. Instead of pressing charges, she helped to broker a deal to help the teen work in the store to pay back damages.</p><h3><b>Education</b></h3><p>Stratton graduated from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1987 with a bachelor’s degree in broadcast journalism. She grew up in the Pill Hill neighborhood and went to Kenwood Academy High School. Her first elected office was parent representative and later chair of the Kenwood Academy Local School Council.</p><h3><b>AKA</b></h3><p>Stratton is a member of Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, the country’s first intercollegiate Black sorority, which was founded in 1908 at Howard University. It’s part of a group of historically Black sororities and fraternities commonly known as the “Divine Nine.” AKA now has more than 1,000 chapters and over 300,000 initiated members worldwide. The organization’s headquarters is on the South Side of Chicago at 5656 S. Stony Island Ave. Former Vice President Kamala Harris and U.S. Rep. Lauren Underwood are also members of the sorority.</p><h3><b>South Side bites</b></h3><p>Stratton lives in Bronzeville and frequents South Side restaurants and bakeries, including Virtue in Hyde Park, Brown Sugar Bakery in Greater Grand Crossing, Ain’t She Sweet Cafe in Bronzeville and Strugglebeard in Hyde Park. entries.title: NFL commissioner, Bears execs met with Illinois legislators about stadium
entries.summary: <p>NFL commissioner Roger Goodell joined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> chairman George McCaskey and president/CEO Kevin Warren in a meeting with Illinois legislators this week, a source confirmed, leaving open future discussions about a stadium site in either Chicago or the suburbs. </p><p>The Bears said in a statement Friday they “appreciate the recent engagement from Illinois leadership to explore legislation, which has allowed us to share our feedback.”</p><p>The Bears’ Illinois flirtation is in advance of the fall veto session, which begins Nov. 17 in Springfield. No deal can happen until then — and it’s unclear whether the Bears, even with their red-hot status on the field, would be atop of legislative priority list. The Bears’ stadium search has dragged on for five-and-a-half years.</p><p>Goodell met with Illinois politicians in August, too, and later said that “we want to make sure that Arlington Heights and Illinois have an opportunity, and Indiana as well, to put their best foot forward.” A month later, he joined Gov. JB Prtizker and Bears minority owner Pat Ryan in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/10/01/nfl-commissioner-roger-goodell-illinois-visit-bears-stadium-talks-gov-jb-pritzker" target="_blank" >another meeting</a> with legislators. The commissioner would not have been involved in such discussions unless the Bears were interested in remaining in Illinois.</p><p>Different city sites have pitched renderings of Bears stadiums to the public in recent weeks, one at Rate Field site and another at the former U.S. Steel South Works. The Bears are unaffiliated with either.</p><p>The Bears also said Friday they’ll continue to work with Indiana leaders and are finalizing the details of two different sites in the Wolf Lake area of Hammond, for which they’ve pledged $2 billion. The team’s board of directors voted in June to move forward with those plans, though no one ruled out building in Arlington Heights, where the Bears own a 326-acre property. Legislation to lower the Bears’ Arlington Heights property taxes flopped in the legislature’s spring sessions.</p><p>Pritzker on Friday called the meetings "part of a continuing endeavor" to get ready for the veto session. </p><p>"We want to make sure the legislation is ready for people to look at and maybe have some hearings during that first week," he said. "And then hopefully get voted on during the second week of veto."</p><p>Pritzker didn't expect Illinois House Speaker Emanuel "Chris" Welch's surprising ouster to disrupt negotiations.</p><p>"We're on track," he said. "We've got leaders other than the speaker involved in the House of Representatives as well as in the Senate. So things are moving apace."</p>
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Falta de resultados impide declarar ganadores en dos distritos de la Junta de Educación de Chicago
entries.summary: <p>La Junta Electoral de Chicago sigue contando votos, lo que mantiene en suspenso el destino de dos contiendas por la Junta de Educación.</p><p>Los votos emitidos el martes en casi todas las casillas de la ciudad han sido reportados por la junta electoral, incluidos los votos del 44.6% de los votantes registrados, es decir, 686,000 habitantes de Chicago.</p><p>Pero hasta la noche del jueves, 12 de 1,291 casillas no se habían contabilizado, comparado a 50 casillas el miércoles.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ae0000" name="module-ae0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La junta contó 12,000 votos adicionales el jueves, mostró el análisis de WBEZ. Hay <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/news/uncounted-ballot-reporting-2026-midterm-general-election" target="_blank" >3,000 boletas del día de las elecciones por contar</a>, según la junta, y 131,131 votos sin contar en total, incluidas las boletas por correo. Más de 4,000 boletas provisionales también quedan por tabular.</p><p>Cuando WBEZ preguntó por qué estaban ocurriendo demoras en el conteo de las boletas del día de las elecciones, un portavoz de la junta dijo que hay “transmisiones continuas a nuestro sistema central de ingreso de datos y tabulación”.</p><p>Este contratiempo significa que los resultados de las contiendas en los distritos escolares 5b y 7a, en el lado oeste, por ahora, siguen siendo demasiado ajustados para declararlos. Otros dos distritos, 3b y 6a, que abarcan el lado norte y el centro, tampoco han sido declarados aunque todas las casillas han reportado resultados. En ambos distritos, menos de 240 votos separan a los dos candidatos con más votos.</p><p>Hasta la tarde del jueves, Jason Dónes encabezaba a su oponente, Carlos Rivas Jr., en la contienda del distrito 3b, pero sólo por 127 votos. No se habían contado los votos de cuatro de las 74 casillas del distrito, que sumaban poco más de 4,000 votantes registrados.</p><p>Con los datos publicados por la junta la noche del jueves, Dónes aumentó su ventaja por apenas 53 votos.</p><p>“Estamos al frente, no vamos detrás, pero la cosa cambia”, dijo Dónes el jueves al mediodía, mientras hacía una pausa en el trabajo, que describió como una buena distracción. “Pero llámame en 30 minutos y tal vez haya bajado. Vuelve a llamar y quizá haya aumentado... Son unos días aterradores. Todos están prendiendo una veladora”.</p><p>Los funcionarios electorales tienen hasta el 17 de noviembre para terminar de contar las boletas por correo y las boletas provisionales. Los resultados oficiales finales deben publicarse el 24 de noviembre.</p><p>En la contienda del distrito 5b, en el lado oeste, Michilla “Kyla” Blaise tiene una ventaja mayor sobre el opositor Anthony Hargrove, de 1,302 votos. Los totales publicados la noche del jueves mostraron que quedaba solo una casilla por contabilizar<b>.</b> Más temprano en el día, ese distrito tenía cuatro casillas sin contar, una de ellas dividida entre los distritos 5b y 7a.</p><p>No está claro si el mismo problema afectó a todas las casillas faltantes. En las casillas del distrito 5b, el problema habría sido, según Blaise, una discrepancia entre un conteo realizado por una máquina contadora electrónica y otro realizado a mano por un juez electoral.</p><p>El abogado de Blaise le indicó que los jueces estaban revisando las boletas y que esperaba alguna resolución para la tarde del jueves.</p><p>“Asumo que, ya sabes, esas personas llevan como 13 o 14 horas ahí, y alguien rellenó mal algo en un espacio en blanco”, dijo. “No creo que sea una crisis, pero agradezco que estén siendo minuciosos”.</p><p>Mientras tanto, la Junta de Elecciones está evaluando una escasez de boletas que contribuyó a las largas filas para votar el día de las elecciones. El problema se debió en parte a un error de computación que calculó mal el número de boletas necesarias en cada casilla, según un comunicado de la junta la noche del jueves. No se sabe si eso está afectando la publicación de los resultados de las contiendas y no se indicó que así fuera.</p><p>La junta también señaló un “aumento significativo” en las inscripciones de votantes el mismo día en las casillas, más de 34,000 personas, el segundo total más alto en la historia de la ciudad.</p><p><i>Contribuyó: Sarah Karp </i><br><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>
entries.author: Cam Rodriguez

entries.title: Bulls need to start thinking differently about rebuild; look to trade
entries.summary: <p>It’s still way too early to call the experiment a complete failure but it is time to start re-evaluating the thought behind it.</p><p>Not that the bottom-half teams of the NBA talent pool were wrong in the strategy on paper. However, as often in analytics and letting too many of the nerds in, paper doesn’t take into account human nature and feel.</p><p>It doesn’t fully weigh the competitive side of a Norman Powell.</p><p>The Bulls need to and soon.</p><p>Like a handful of franchises, the Bulls looked at the new 3-2-1 draft lottery system and realized finishing in the bottom three was now rolling snake eyes, while positions 4-10 were the sweet spot. The NBA wanted to discourage tanking so the first seven teams outside the bottom three have the best odds at the No. 1 pick. The bottom three have the same odds (5.4%) as play-in teams.</p><p>The other important caveat in the new system is a team cannot win the No. 1 overall pick in back-to-back seasons and can’t be in the top five three consecutive years.</p><p>It was the NBA saying, “OK, get in and get out.”</p><p>So the likes of the Bulls added an All-Star vet like Powell to make sure they were good-bad. Just as Brooklyn added a Julius Randle and held onto Michael Porter Jr., Sacramento kept veterans Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis, and Utah surprised everyone at the trade deadline by acquiring Jaren Jackson Jr. last February.</p><p>Bad teams that wanted a vet to keep them afloat outside the bottom three, and in Utah’s case maybe even higher.</p><p>Powell is more than just an organizational life preserver. Same with Randle. These are highly competitive vets that want to do the right thing but also need to get their numbers and keep themselves relevant on the trade market.</p><p>They understand the business of basketball.</p><p>So if Powell is taking questionable three-pointers early in the shot clock – the words of Bulls coach Tiago Splitter – don’t hate the player, hate the game front offices are trying to play.</p><p>Meanwhile, Memphis is playing the competitive basketball the Bulls, Kings, Jazz and Nets were hoping to play by simply having a former Sixth Man of the Year candidate in Ty Jerome supplement their two last top draft picks Cameron Boozer and Cedric Coward.</p><p>They’re not suffocating the youth movement by relying on an All-Star to act as a buoy.</p><p>To Powell’s credit, he is trying to balance helping the young guys get theirs but also get his own.</p><p>“We’ve got to do a better job of competing,” Powell said of the uncompetitive basketball being played in a 1-7 start. “We’ve got to have some heart out there, some mental toughness, some fortitude to bring a compete level. Teams are coming in, looking at us like it's lunch.”</p><p>And the Bulls have been making sure lunch is served. Almost daily.</p><p>What they now need to start wrapping their minds – and analytics department – around is come December, aggressively exploring new homes for Powell – first and foremost – as well as Isaac Okoro, Tre Jones and Jalen Smith.</p><p>This 2027 draft class is not worthy of chasing a No. 1 at the expense of clearing a better runway for Caleb Wilson and Matas Buzelis to develop. They need to take what they can get from it and position themselves in that 4-10 range for a more talented ’28 class. Then reassess where the rebuild is.</p><p>Better results are coming for the Bulls just with the schedule about to lighten up and veteran center Nic Claxton (hamstring) set to make his season debut on Sunday. That shouldn’t matter. Roster construction is not an exact science even though teams are dumping millions into a strategy department to try and tell them it is.</p><p>The NBA is still a player-first business.</p><p>In the case of the Bulls, that business needs to pick up.</p>
entries.author: Joe Cowley

entries.title: Gunman commandeers CTA bus with passengers through Southwest Side, prosecutors say
entries.summary: <p>A man who hijacked a CTA bus with passengers while waving a loaded gun around and demanding its driver to run four red lights through several neighborhoods on the Southwest Side earlier this week remains behind bars Friday. </p><p>Quentin Lewis, 36 and of the Garfield Park neighborhood, was charged with kidnapping, possessing a weapon as a felon, unlawful restraint and possession of a stolen vehicle, Chicago police said. </p><p>Lewis, who remains in custody at the Cook County Jail, was in court for an initial hearing Thursday, where a judge ordered him detained. </p><p>The chaotic scene began to unfold shortly after Lewis — sporting a gun tucked in the waistband of his shorts — boarded bus #8611 without paying around 8 p.m. Tuesday at Jackson Boulevard and Pulaski Road in the Garfield Park neighborhood, police and prosecutors said. </p><p>Lewis rode along in the southbound bus without incident for about two miles until suddenly, at Pulaski Road and 26th Street in Little Village, he spotted someone who signaled for the driver to pull over "as if to suggest for someone to get off the bus," prosecutors said. </p><p>At that point, Lewis pointed a gun with an extended magazine at that person, who ran for cover and Lewis then demanded the bus driver "go, go, go" south on Pulaski Road as he went back to his seat directly behind the driver, prosecutors said. </p><p>Over the next several minutes and three more miles, Lewis allegedly stood up and waved his gun around while instructing the driver to run red lights, officials said. </p><p>As the bus approached 55th Street and Pulaski Road in the West Elsdon neighborhood, a passenger yanked the emergency lever, which stopped the bus and prevented the driver from moving it further. The two passengers then ran off of the bus, leaving the driver and Lewis alone, officials said. </p><p>The driver, a 35-year-old woman, escaped through the driver's side window and ran toward another CTA bus for help, prosecutors said. </p><p>After "aimlessly" yelling and waving the gun, Lewis also jumped off the bus and ran away, making it to a nearby strip mall where he got into the driver's seat of a Dodge Ram pickup truck that was still running, while its driver was inside a bakery buying bread, officials said. </p><p>Police caught up with him there and ordered him to drop the gun and get out of the pickup. He did but not before he placed the truck in reverse, causing it to slam into a police car. He was placed under arrest about 8:25 p.m. </p><p>A Glock firearm, which was loaded with one round in the chamber and an unknown amount of live rounds in an extended magazine, was recovered from the Dodge, officials said. </p><p>Lewis, who is a convicted felon with no CCL or FOID, was identified in a photo array by the bus driver and one of the witnesses, prosecutors said. He is due back in court on Nov. 10, records show. </p>

entries.title: Gov. Pritzker to undergo second medical procedure, pause public duties while recovering
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker is once again undergoing an out-patient urology procedure on Monday that will take him away from public events as he recovers, the governor's office said on Friday.</p><p>The procedure is the "standard and final follow-up to the same procedure he completed in May 2026," spokesman Matt Hill said. </p><p>"The Governor will continue fulfilling his duties and pause public events while recovering," Hill said. "The Governor is grateful for well-wishes and looks forward to resuming public events soon.”</p><p>Pritzker on May 1 underwent a "routine outpatient urology procedure" and stepped back from public duties. The governor's office then said he would be fulfilling his "duties" but would pause public events. </p><p>The disclosure comes three days after Pritzker won his third term as Illinois governor, defeating Republican candidate Darren Bailey by nearly 23 points. It was Pritzker's widest margin of victory yet while becoming Illinois’ first Democrat elected to a third term as governor and the first in more than a century to carry McHenry County, the most conservative collar county, as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/blue-tsunami-democrats-massive-advantage-illinois-general-assembly" target="_blank" ><u>blue tsunami washed through Springfield</u></a>, too.</p><p>The Democratic governor in September publicly disclosed that he had<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/09/21/illinois-governor-jb-pritzker-interview-glp-1-diabetes-weight-loss" target="_blank" > lost 80 pounds</a> with the help of a GLP-1 and exercise. In an interview with the Sun-Times, Pritzker said that he would be open to sharing health information with the public "if there's anything that threatens my life."</p><p>"I think the public has to know that. I think that people don't need to know every little thing about my health," Pritzker said. "I don't think sending out my cholesterol levels... I don't have a problem. I'll let people know if I do. I think it's private information, but it shouldn't be private if it's going to affect my job and my ability to do my job. But that is a point at which I think the public deserves to know, whether it's my job or my longevity, while I would be governor, I think the public should know." </p><p>All of the focus on Pritzker's health and weight comes as he continues to appear on the list of potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders. He once again dodged a question about a White House bid on Wednesday as he offered a congressional agenda in wake of the blue wave that swept the country. </p><p>“Everything, including the agenda that we put forward today and everything we’ve done in the last eight years, has really been about the people of Illinois,” Pritzker said. “What is good for the people of Illinois? Those are the questions that I ask every day. When I wake up in the morning, what am I gonna do to make people’s lives better?"</p>
entries.author: Tina Sfondeles

entries.title: Doggonit! City dog licensing hits an all-time low
entries.summary: <p>Chicago’s bark has long been worse than its bite when it comes to cracking down on owners of unlicensed dogs, but there now appears to be no bite at all.</p><p>That much was obvious Friday when City Clerk Anna Valencia revealed during City Council budget hearings that her office has issued only 4,100 dog licenses this year in a city with an estimated dog population of more than 650,000.</p><p>That’s down from the already paltry 8,000 dog licenses last year, 18,000 in 2017 and 40,896 in 2013.</p><p>The cost of a city dog license is clearly not the impediment.</p><p>The license fee has been frozen for decades at $5 a year for spayed and neutered dogs, $50 for those that are not and $2.50 for dog owners who are senior citizens.</p><p>Valencia said the problem is ignorance. The city’s regulatory leash has been so loose for so long, most Chicago dog owners don’t even know that they’re required to buy city licenses for their dogs.</p><p>“People don’t know. And if you don’t have a marketing budget to tell people, they just don’t understand,” Valencia told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“There’s no marketing dollars. You can do as much free marketing as possible, which we have, but there’s 2.7 million people in this city. We’ve done some free PSA [public service announcement] stuff. That’s important, but it’s not gonna be enough to move the needle.”</p><p>Downtown Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) said the number of dog licenses issued by the city is “ridiculously low” because it has “never been a priority” for the city to enforce the legal requirement — even on the city’s own agencies.</p><p>Reilly said the city’s Commission on Animal Care and Control transfers roughly 10,000 dogs to adoption partners like PAWS and the Anti-Cruelty Society without issuing dog licenses before transferring the animals.</p><p>“The vast majority of dog owners want to comply with city laws, but many are unaware that the city even requires a license. The city should not be imposing licensing requirements without properly educating the public regarding their obligations,” Reilly told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“This has been an issue for decades and it appears compliance has dropped off even further. I asked the city clerk to make this a priority through a public education campaign that leverages free public service announcement air time on local TV and radio, as well as the city’s massive network of JCDecaux billboards, bus shelter ads and video kiosks.”</p><p>Ald. Ray Lopez (15th), the City Council’s resident dog lover, said the 4,100 dog licenses sold by the city — at a time when Cook County issues 500,000 annual rabies tags — shows that there is a “breakdown in communication that’s hurting the city’s ability to fully track” stray dogs.</p><p>“It’s not just about the revenue. It helps with identification and the return-to-owner law. If your pet escapes and has a valid city license tag on it, we’ll bring that pup home for free. It won’t go to Animal Care and Control because we’ll know where that dog belongs,” Lopez said.</p><p>“That’s the greatest value of the dog license. If one of my dogs were to escape, anyone could scan and see where that dog lives, bring him home and I don’t have to worry about him going to the pound." </p><p>Currently, dog owners can obtain a dog license at the city clerk's office or through the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicityclerk.com/dog-registration" target="_blank" >city’s clerk web site</a>. But for years, dog owners who failed to purchase dog licenses have gotten a pass.</p><p>That changed in 2005, when the clerk's office put computer software in place to match its short list of licensed dogs with Cook County's larger list of Chicago dogs with rabies shots. </p><p>Warning letters were then mailed to those whose names appeared on the county's list, but not the city's, prompting a small boost in registration. </p><p>That's the way it stayed until October 2011, when then-City Clerk Susana Mendoza's outreach campaign and the threat of tickets prompted a larger surge in dog registrations.</p><p>On Friday, Lopez proposed requiring animal hospitals and veterinarians to purchase city dog licenses in advance like they do rabies tags, and issue them "at the point of vaccination."</p><p>"Administer this tax as they would a sales tax in a retail environment,” Lopez said.</p><p>Valencia proposed a "universal dog license" that would be issued jointly by the city and the Chicago Park District. </p><p>“The Park District offers a dog license and we do. Instead of overlapping, we should do one together and split the cost. But we can’t do that until we get our new technology system," she said.</p><p>Valencia made no apologies for letting dog licensing slide in favor of higher priorities: amnesty programs that give people debt relief; City Key IDs that help them get housing and enroll kids in school, and City Council modernization.</p><p>"We only have so many people and so many resources," she said.</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: Political groups spent $12 million to defeat CTU candidates. One losing race cost $76 per vote.
entries.summary: <p>Political spending groups funded by an area billionaire seeking to defeat the Chicago Teachers Union in historic school board elections on Tuesday may have won their preferred president, thanks to their infusion of millions.</p><p>But in several school board district races, they spent their biggest money per vote — only for those candidates to lose, a Chicago Sun-Times analysis has found.</p><p>Common Ground Collective, which shelled out the most money by far through Nov. 2 — about $7 million — spent as much as $45 per vote to sway unsuccessful district races. Most of the cash spent by its political action committee and super PAC came from powerful billionaire <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/16/michael-sacks-profile-chicago-billionaire-mayoral-race-brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-rahm-emanuel" target="_blank" ><u>Michael Sacks</u></a>.</p><p>In District 1b on the Northwest Side, the $473,000 it spent bolstering Michelle Pierre and attacking her opponent, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-district-1b-results" target="_blank" ><u>who ultimately prevailed</u></a>. That’s $43 per vote.</p><p>Similar trends held true for the cash-rich Illinois Network of Charter Schools, whose $4.4 million spending also funded costly defeats — as much as $31 a vote, according to an analysis of PAC and super PAC spending through Nov. 2 and vote totals available Nov. 5.</p><p>The big piles of cash that poured into the inaugural full board elections came mainly through independent super PACs that have no contribution or spending limits — and cannot coordinate with candidates. Through Nov. 2, spending aimed against CTU candidates by these two groups totaled $11.5 million. Another group consistently spending against CTU candidates,The Urban Center, bumps the total to $11.9 million.<b> </b></p><p>The money aims to counteract the CTU’s built-in advantages — incumbency, an army of workers and established connections with some voters who are or were Chicago Public Schools parents.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-450000" name="html-embed-module-450000"></a><div style="min-height:426px" id="datawrapper-vis-4R5AQ"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/4R5AQ/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-4R5AQ"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/4R5AQ/full.png" alt="Did spending big to oppose CTU candidates pay off in key races? (Split Bars)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>But the money hardly guaranteed victory, and some candidates worry it backfired.</p><p>Pierre says the public confused the super PAC spending on her behalf with her own values — and voted as many Americans did Tuesday against candidates backed by the mega-wealthy.</p><p>“That definitely did not represent me,” the long-time educator says. “But that narrative was shared constantly. This narrative of billionaires intervening in elections probably had an impact.”</p><p>Both groups that sought to declaw the CTU did not manage to win a decisive majority. Though <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/05/missing-election-day-results-holding-up-race-calls-in-two-chicago-school-board-districts" target="_blank" ><u>four races remain too close to call</u></a>, CTU-backed candidates could win as many as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/11/03/chicago-teachers-union-poised-to-capture-half-of-school-board-district-seats-but-likely-to-lose-presidency" target="_blank" ><u>10 of 20 seats</u></a>.</p><p>However, the two super PACs’ combined $4.6 million for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-president-results" target="_blank" ><u>Jessica Biggs for president</u></a> appears to have paid off. They spent about $16 per vote, $13 of that from Common Ground, a new political group that aims to “defeat extremist efforts from both the far right and far left that seek to divide our city.”</p><p>Asked at a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/14/4-takeaways-from-cps-school-board-president-forum" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ campaign forum</u></a> about the big money backing her, Biggs, who is a current board member, answered the question by leaning on her “voting record that shows my independence.”</p><p>Common Ground’s director Chuck Swirsky argues that come January, the union will be down from its current 15 members who were elected with CTU’s backing or appointed by ally Mayor Brandon Johnson, plus, their candidate for president,<b> </b>“Hilario Dominguez lost big — it's a clear repudiation by the voters and the kids are worth it every time."</p><p>The $16-per-vote to boost Biggs is a bargain compared to some district candidates who lost.</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-3fbf6c24-da29-11f1-9f12-fd7b98683e86"><li>Spending on Peter Gonzales’ loss in near Northwest Side <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-district-3a-results" target="_blank" ><u>district 3a</u></a> broke down to about $76 per vote. </li><li>Spending on Pierre’s loss in District 1b farther out on the Northwest Side broke down to about $71 per vote. </li><li>For Jesus Ayala Jr. in southwestern district 7a, each vote equaled $56 in outside spending. That race <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-district-7a-results" target="_blank" ><u>remains too close to call</u></a>, with the CTU-endorsed candidate leading.</li></ul><p>By contrast the CTU spent less than $4 per vote in these winning races. CTU PAC and Our Schools PAC, the two supporting union candidates, spent more than $2.6 million through Nov. 2, according to state board of elections filings. CTU has no super PAC.</p><p>Gonzales points to campaign finance law letting super PACs fund ads as long as they act separately from campaigns.</p><p>“That wasn't anything to do with us, and we noticed this at the polls. People kept saying this, that we were somehow funded by Michael Sacks,” he says. “I've never met Michael Sacks … I didn't take any money from Michael Sacks.”</p><p>Paralegal and CPS parent Connie Anderson <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-district-10b-results" target="_blank" ><u>in District 10b on the South Side</u></a> fought her discouragement about disparate spending — about $50 per vote for her opponent vs less than $3 for her from CTU.</p><p>“Every day … another ad will come out, and another lie will come out and you're just like, ‘I don't know what I got myself into’, ” she said Tuesday night, declaring victory. “Then lo and behold, you're looking at the polls, and you're like, ‘Wait, what? People believe in my platform’.”</p><p>The anti-CTU spending did pay off in a few key races, including <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-district-5a-results" target="_blank" ><u>the upset of incumbent Aaron “Jitu” Brown</u></a>, an activist and catalyst behind the law that changed the board to an elected one.</p><p>It also helped keep retired school psychologist Therese Boyle in her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-district-9b-results" target="_blank" ><u>Southwest Side 9a board seat</u></a>, with anti-CTU groups spending only $2 more per vote.</p><p>The $590,000 behind ads attacking Brown and promoting real estate agent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/voter-guide-midterm-election-illinois/illinois-midterm-results-2026/chicago-school-board-district-5a/" target="_blank" ><u>LaPamela Williams</u></a>, who did not return messages for comment, in West Side District 5a equaled $57 per vote.</p><p>“So I definitely think the money played a role because it was not a race where they were promoting ... my opponent,” Brown says. “It was an anti-Jitu Brown race.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Justin Myers, Sun-Times, and Sarah Karp, WBEZ</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-790000" name="module-790000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Chicago School Board election results</b><br><ul id="rte-99ebbb22-d88c-11f1-a0f8-2966deb425a8"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-president-results" >Jessica Biggs wins president race</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-teachers-union-poised-to-capture-half-of-school-board-district-seats-but-likely-to-lose-presidency" target="_blank" >CTU poised to capture half of school board district seats, but loses president’s race</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-results" target="_blank" >What you need to know about all 21 races</a></li></ul></div> </div><p></p>
