entries.title: Developers pitching 28-story apartment tower in Lake View
entries.summary: <p>Three Chicago companies are proposing a 28-story apartment tower that would transform the bustling corner at North Sheridan Road and West Diversey Parkway.</p><p>Antunovich Associates, Continuum Development and Chicago Development Partners presented plans for redeveloping the vacant Ida and Norman Stone Medical Building at 2800 N. Sheridan Road, during a virtual community meeting Wednesday night. </p><p>“I think it is obvious to the neighborhood that it's just such a … critical gateway location between Lincoln Park — both the neighborhood as well as the park itself — and the Lake View community,” Patrick Cusack, principal at Antunovich Associates, said. “What we were hoping to do was bring something a little bit new into Lake View. This is meant to be a very, very high-quality residential building and really speak to the quality of the neighborhood, and just bring some activity to this corner that, unfortunately, was just not well activated with the medical office building.”</p><p>Demolition of the Lake View building is already underway and should be complete by the end of the year, according to the development team.</p><p>The building will have 345 apartments, including 69 affordable units for households earning between $50,000 and $70,000 annually, as mandated under the city’s Affordable Requirements Ordinance.</p><p>The apartments will include a mix of studios, convertibles and one- to three-bedrooms, with some units also having a den. The apartments will range from 500 square feet for a studio up to about 1,600 square feet for a three-bedroom.</p><p>Monthly rent for studios will start at $2,700. A three-bedroom, depending on the size, could rent between $8,000 to $10,000, Continuum Development co-founder Evan Meador said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ef0000" name="image-ef0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/523e381/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1816x1019+0+92/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4e%2Ffd%2F8df855544a0d8364c75a3480721e%2F2800nsheridan-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/19fc733/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1816x1019+0+92/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4e%2Ffd%2F8df855544a0d8364c75a3480721e%2F2800nsheridan-3.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a2da084/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1816x1019+0+92/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4e%2Ffd%2F8df855544a0d8364c75a3480721e%2F2800nsheridan-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Rendering of 2800 N. The development team said it secured a fitness club for the space but declined to say who.</p><p>An additional 10,000 square feet of retail and commercial space is planned. The development team said it originally explored anchoring the building with a grocer — but the tight alleyways and traffic congestion at the intersection didn’t make it feasible. Instead, they're exploring a boutique market concept for the retail space, Meador said.</p><p>There will also be a pool deck for residents, 275 parking spaces and 345 bike spaces. Parking is intended for residents and fitness club members, according to the development team. </p><p>The project has been a long time in the making. The developers held their first community meeting with South East Lake View Neighbors on Nov. 10, 2025. SELVN will vote on Monday whether to support the development.</p><p>Several neighbors at Wednesday's meeting praised the development team for building more housing at a time when Chicagoans desperately need it. A few asked about the building’s size, which the developers said is in scale with nearby high-rises that frame Diversey Harbor. For example, the buildings at 340 and 330 W. Diversey Parkway are 27 stories tall and 2650 N. Lakeview Ave. is 44 floors.</p><p>“We recognize this is a prominent Lake View site, and a project of this scale needs to respond very thoughtfully to its surroundings,” Cusack said.</p>

entries.title: White Sox enter GM meetings with a shorter runway for a vital offseason
entries.summary: <p>Five years ago, the now-familiar specter of oncoming MLB lockout drove a free-agent frenzy at the end of November. The Cubs signed two-time All-Star Marcus Stroman, the Blue Jays landed a staff ace in Kevin Gausman, the Rangers committed a half-billion dollars to a double play combination of Marcus Semien and Corey Seager that delivered a World Series championship.</p><p>On the South Side, the White Sox added setup man Kendall Graveman around Thanksgiving, but the last-minute deal they snuck under the wire was a three-year pact to retain utilityman Leury Garcia after his career-best 2021 campaign. In his Zoom presser held hours before the curtain fell on MLB transactions for months, the amiable Garcia professed ignorance about the nearing lockout. The Sox released Garcia in spring of 2023.</p><p>It’s likely, and maybe even ideal, that neither bit of history is that instructive of a preview of how the White Sox will navigate this unusual winter.</p><p>Chris Getz was the assistant general manager the last time a labor crisis was dropped in the middle of an offseason that was supposed to see the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/30/white-sox-face-a-new-challenge-this-winter-improving-a-contender" target="_blank" ><u>Sox improve upon a promising roster that was felled in the ALDS</u></a>. Maybe different insight he took from that experience will reveal themselves with time, but the primary one he espoused last month was a reminder to be ready for anything.</p><p>“You are at the mercy of other clubs and how they're going about their business, certainly agents and players,” Getz said. “I think the biggest lesson is just being as prepared as possible.”</p><p>Back in 2019, catcher Yasmani Grandal’s face-to-face meeting with Sox leadership during the General Managers’ meetings swiftly evolved into a four-year deal announced before Thanksgiving. More often, next week’s gathering of MLB decision-makers striding through a Las Vegas resort in high-end athleisure is the first time clubs can tout a fully-formed idea of their offseason needs, and the next three-to-four months are spent tracking them down.</p><p>Typically, teams are just emerging from their internal meetings during this time. They’ve been filling staff positions, exemplified by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/29/white-sox-hiring-matt-roffe-away-from-brewers-to-fill-open-amateur-scouting-director-role" target="_blank" ><u>the Sox hiring new amateur scouting director Matt Roffe</u></a>, and now needing to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/04/white-sox-assistant-hitting-coach-joel-mckeithan-departing-for-promotion-with-cardinals" target="_blank" ><u>replace assistant hitting coach Joel McKeithan</u></a>. They’ve been imparting offseason development plans to their players, especially since they’re about to lose contact with members of the 40-man roster. Those conversations include the determination of whether Grant Taylor is headed to the rotation or remaining in the bullpen, which the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/04/grant-taylor-is-carrying-the-white-sox-this-postseason-will-he-do-it-as-a-starter-in-the-future-kyle-teel-chris-getz-will-venable-brian-bannister-zach-bove" target="_blank" ><u>right-hander reaffirmed to the Sun-Times last month</u></a> would be discussed after the postseason.</p><p>“Everything’s gone to plan in trying to get to a certain amount of innings this year,” Taylor said last month about his progress toward preseason goals for building him near a starter’s workload.</p><p>Last year at the GM meetings, Getz spent his media session tamping down speculation on potential trade candidates among his positional core, projecting the promotion timeline for top outfield prospect Braden Montgomery, and clarifying Taylor’s role. This year, he could easily do the same and just swap out Caleb Bonemer for Montgomery, or add Hagen Smith to the discussion of invaluable multi-inning relievers/unproven potential starters. With Manager of the Year and Executive of the Year awards being handed out on Nov. 10 and 11 respectively, there could be one more chance to reflect on the accomplishments of 2026 as well.</p><p>There’s a natural pacing to the MLB offseason that a December lockout is going to waylay. Without the winter meetings to drive player movement that month, can teams speed up their process so that the GM meetings serve as a substitute?</p><p>By the Sox’ own telling of the progression, they were weeks away from viewing Munetaka Murakami as a realistic possibility at this point last November. But in retrospect, Getz’s description of a need for a left-handed infield help who didn’t necessarily need to be able to play third base already matched the Japanese slugger, less than a week after he had been posted by the Yakult Swallows.</p><p>Japanese players who have been posted by their current clubs have already been made to adjust, as The Athletic reported that the 45-day window to sign will not be paused for the lockout, and the likes of NPB Triple Crown winner Teruaki Sato will need to pick a MLB team before the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1. If knowledge of the market is the issue, after a trade deadline where they lacked the middle-class prospect depth to comfortably swing deals, and a contending season that made pulling from the big league roster in trades less palatable, the Sox have had reason to be sizing up the free-agent crop for a while now.</p><p>“We don’t have the bullets that we have like when we first got here,” assistant general manager Josh Barfield said in September. “We had three [2 WAR] or better players in that [Garrett] Crochet deal. It gets harder and harder, as you get better.”</p><p>It gets harder and the stakes are higher, but the strength of an overall weak free-agent class is largely rooted in the starting pitching the Sox desperately need. Outside of Tarik Skubal, most of the options are gettable for less than the five years, $125 million they were willing to offer Zack Wheeler in December of 2019.</p><p>As weird and unusual as this offseason might get, the White Sox have been here before. The only rub is they have to get it right this time.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Bears 'maniac' Rome Odunze trending toward his best season
entries.summary: <p>Standing in a raucous <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> locker room Monday night, receiver Kalif Raymond was asked what he saw on the screen pass that he took 39 yards in the fourth quarter to seal the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/03/bears-seahawks-quarterback-caleb-williams-masters-elaborate-gameplan-nfl" target="_blank" >34-17 win against the Seahawks</a>.</p><p>“Rome Odunze,” he said.</p><p>Odunze was stacked in front of Raymond on third-and-nine from the Seahawks’ 44 with the Bears holding a suddenly precarious three-point lead.</p><p>Right tackle Darnell Wright let edge rusher DeMarcus Lawrence sprint in toward quarterback Caleb Williams, who had to sidearm the ball around him, so he could race out to block safety Nick Emmanwori. Right guard Jonah Jackson blocked just enough of linebacker Ernest Jones to slow him down.</p><p>Odunze sealed off cornerback Josh Jobe, pushing him toward the sideline. Raymond ran through the tunnel for the huge gain.</p><p>“If [Odunze] doesn’t get that block, the screen doesn’t go,” Raymond said.</p><p>He wasn’t surprised.</p><p>“He does it every single time. …” Raymond said. “That dude is a maniac.”</p><p>The Bears didn’t draft Odunze ninth overall for his blocking prowess. When they weigh whether to extend his contract — as soon as this upcoming offseason — they’ll look more at receiving yards than the dirty work he does.</p><p>The combination of the two, though, is compelling. Entering Sunday night's game against the Buccaneers, Odunze is on pace for the best season of his three-year career.</p><p>“I’m on a mission to become a complete wide receiver …” Odunze said. “Whether that’s blocking, catching passes, YAC [yards after catch], incredible spectacular catches, whatever that is, I’m trying to do a lot of those different things. Blocking is a part of that, especially in this offense, and I’m trying to be excellent at it.”</p><p>His production is ticking up, too, and it’s about time.</p><p>In his first three games, Odunze caught eight passes on 13 targets for 139 yards. In the five since, he’s caught 20 passes on 31 targets for 329.</p><p>“The ball’s finding me,” he said.</p><p>That hasn’t always been the case.</p><p>Odunze was hampered by a popgun passing attack in his rookie year, posting just 734 receiving yards. Hampered by a chronic foot injury last year, he had just 661.</p><p>This season, he’s on pace for 994 receiving yards. In a league where 19 players had 1,000 or more last season, that’s more in line with the Bears’ expectations.</p><p>Odunze does what the Bears’ other pass-catchers can’t — he’s their deep threat. He’s 10<sup>th</sup> in the NFL in targeted air yards, which measures how far the ball flies in the air on passes in his direction. Luther Burden, the next-highest-ranked Bear, is 76<sup>th</sup>.</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson’s offense doesn’t try to feed one receiver, or focus on one at a given time. Amazingly, Odunze has 14 catches for 234 yards in the first half this season — and 14 catches for 234 yards in the second. In addition to Odunze, receiver Luther Burden, tight end Colston Loveland, running back D’Andre Swift and Raymond have all led the team in receiving in a game this season.</p><p>“Sometimes that’s how it is when you have so many good play-makers out on the field,” Odunze said. “Sometimes there can be different lulls in getting the ball or not.”</p><p>Williams has thrived in his second season throwing to Burden and Loveland and his third throwing to Odunze.</p><p>“That’s big,” Williams said. “The communication, our relationship as a group has grown. We hang out together. We do things together. We eat together, break bread together. … You start building that relationship and that bond between each other.</p><p>“They’re super-talented, so my job is just to put the ball in the area and try to give them the best ball I can each and every time.”</p><p> Receivers, of course, would rather be known for what they do with the ball in their hands. Odunze won’t apologize for wanting it.</p><p>“We got a bunch of ballplayers,” he said. “We all want the ball. You can ask every receiver around the league, ‘Who wants more targets?’ And they’ll say, ‘Me.’”</p><p>Johnson has a saying, though — “No block, no rock.”</p><p>“It's all in between the ears as much as anything else,” Johnson said. “And that's what we try to evaluate when guys are coming out of college, because they're not asked to do it a whole lot. You can get the technique and the fundamentals better through coaching, and yet you need to see that willingness to put their face in there and get dirty…</p><p>“If you're not doing that part of it, then it's hard to have you out there. It's a big part of our offense.”</p><p>Rewarding Odunze with the ball makes sense.</p><p>“That's the perfect scenario for us,” Johnson said.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley
